- dotnet-backend-patterns: Master C#/.NET backend development patterns for building robust APIs, MCP servers, and enterprise applications. Covers async/await, dependency injection, Entity Framework Core, Dapper, configuration, caching, and testing with xUnit. Use when developing .NET backends, reviewing C# code, or designing API architectures.
- find-skills
- kubernetes: Expert in Kubernetes and DevOps with infrastructure-as-code and cloud-native patterns
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

The fix is complete. Here's a summary of what was wrong and what I changed.

## Root cause

The pod logs show Ocelot's `DownstreamRouteFinderMiddleware` failing with `UnableToFindDownstreamRouteError` for `GET /ready`:

```
Failed to match Route configuration for upstream path: /ready, verb: GET.
```

The readiness probe hits `/ready` (see `helm-chart-services/templates/backend-service.yaml:49`), but `ocelot.json` has no route for `/ready` — only `/api/v1/*` routes. Since the app was handing unhandled paths to the Ocelot pipeline (`await app.UseOcelot()`), the health-check endpoint never got a chance to handle it; Ocelot swallowed the request and returned the "no route" error, so the readiness probe failed.

Two related problems in `Program.cs`:

1. **`/ready` had no health check registered.** `AddHealthChecks()` only configured URL checks for the *downstream* services — there was no check for the gateway itself, so even if the endpoint were reached it would report Unhealthy.
2. **Ordering was wrong.** `UseHttpsRedirection`, `UseRouting`, `UseAuthorization`, and `UseOcelot()` were called *before* the health-check endpoints were mapped. Ocelot's middleware sits in the pipeline and intercepts `/ready` before the health-check endpoint can respond.

## Changes (`backend/Services/APIGateway/Program.cs`)

- Added a self health check so the gateway reports Healthy on its own readiness probe:
  ```csharp
  .AddCheck("self", () => HealthCheckResult.Healthy())
  ```
- Moved the `MapHealthChecks` and `MapGet`/`MapControllers` endpoint registrations **before** `UseHttpsRedirection`/`UseRouting`/`UseAuthorization`/`UseOcelot()`, so the health endpoints are matched first and Ocelot never sees `/ready`.

## To apply

Rebuild and redeploy the gateway pod:

```
helm upgrade cue-services helm-chart-services -n cue
# or
kubectl rollout restart deployment/cue-services-api-gateway -n cue
```

Then `kubectl get pod -n cue cue-services-api-gateway-* -o wide` and `kubectl logs -n cue <pod>` should show the readiness probe succeeding (no more `UnableToFindDownstreamRouteError` for `/ready`).

# Default values for cue-services.
# This chart manages microservices that are under active development and need frequent deployments.

# Enable/disable infrastructure dependency
infrastructure:
  enabled: false

# Global image settings for all services
global:
  imageRegistry: ""
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

# Backend services common configuration
backend:
  replicaCount: 1
  imageTag: latest
  resources:
    limits:
      memory: 512Mi
      cpu: 500m
    requests:
      memory: 256Mi
      cpu: 250m
  env: {}

# List of backend services
backendServices:
  - name: auth-service
    port: 8080
  - name: user-service
    port: 8080
  - name: profile-service
    port: 8080
  - name: discovery-service
    port: 8080
  - name: booking-service
    port: 8080
  - name: payment-service
    port: 8080
  - name: chat-service
    port: 8080
  - name: notification-service
    port: 8080
  - name: review-service
    port: 8080
  - name: support-service
    port: 8080
  - name: analytics-service
    port: 8080
  - name: api-gateway
    port: 8080

# Frontend configuration
frontend:
  imageTag: latest
  replicaCount: 1
  resources:
    limits:
      memory: 512Mi
      cpu: 500m
    requests:
      memory: 256Mi
      cpu: 250m

# Jaeger configuration (distributed tracing)
jaeger:
  imageTag: "1.47"
  replicaCount: 1
  resources:
    limits:
      memory: 1Gi
      cpu: 500m
    requests:
      memory: 512Mi
      cpu: 250m

# Secret values (to be set by the user, preferably via --set-file or --set-string)
# RAW secrets (no base64 required)
secret:
  # Stripe API key for payments
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: sk_test_421ffVAem5k5Ea8 # placeholder

  # JWT signing key for authentication tokens
  JWT_SIGNING_KEY: supersecretjwtskieforlocal # placeholder

  # Auth Service specific secrets
  JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_MINUTES: "15"
  JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS: "7"

  # Database connection strings (these point to infrastructure services)
  AUTH_DB_CONNECTION: Host=cue-infra-cue-infrastructure-postgres.cue.svc.cluster.local;Port=5432;Database=cue_db;Username=admin;Password=localsecret
  USER_DB_CONNECTION: Host=cue-infra-cue-infrastructure-postgres.cue.svc.cluster.local;Port=5432;Database=cue_db;Username=admin;Password=localsecret
  BOOKING_DB_CONNECTION: Host=cue-infra-cue-infrastructure-postgres.cue.svc.cluster.local;Port=5432;Database=cue_db;Username=admin;Password=localsecret
  PAYMENT_DB_CONNECTION: Host=cue-infra-cue-infrastructure-postgres.cue.svc.cluster.local;Port=5432;Database=cue_db;Username=admin;Password=localsecret
  ConnectionStrings__CueDatabase: Host=cue-infra-cue-infrastructure-postgres.cue.svc.cluster.local;Port=5432;Database=cue_db;Username=admin;Password=localsecret

  # Email service credentials (if using external email provider)
  EMAIL_API_KEY: c2vjcmV0 # placeholder
  EMAIL_FROM_ADDRESS: cue@mailcompany.com

  # Redis connection strings (point to infrastructure Redis)
  REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING: redis://cue-infra-cue-infrastructure-redis.cue.svc.cluster.local:6379

  # RabbitMQ connection (point to infrastructure RabbitMQ)
  RABBITMQ_CONNECTION_STRING: amqp://admin:localsecret@cue-infra-cue-infrastructure-rabbitmq.cue.svc.cluster.local:5672

  # Jaeger tracing endpoint
  JAEGER_AGENT_HOST: jaeger-agent-split-jeager:6831

# Ingress configuration
ingress:
  enabled: false
  className: ""
  annotations: {}
    # kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx
    # kubernetes.io/tls-acme: "true"
  hosts:
    - host: chart-example.local
      paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: ImplementationSpecific
        - path: /api
          pathType: ImplementationSpecific
  tls: []
  #  - secretName: chart-example-tls
  #    hosts:
  #      - chart-example.local

# Service configuration for all services (if needed)
service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 80

# Resource limits and requests can be overridden per service above
resources: {}

# Node labels for pod assignment
nodeSelector: {}

# Tolerations for pod assignment
tolerations: []

# Affinity for pod assignment
affinity: {}

The container's `ocelot.json` is 7175 bytes (the updated version, Sept 6 16:17), but the `APIGateway.dll` is also new (Sept 6 16:25) yet the error still shows. The fact that `/ready` is hitting Ocelot means the health check endpoint mapping **inside the published DLL** still has health endpoints placed after `UseOcelot()`. 

Let me verify: in ASP.NET Core minimal hosting, endpoint registration order vs. middleware order matters differently. In .NET 6+ minimal hosting, `app.MapXxx()` *registers* endpoints, but the routing happens during the request. The actual processing order depends on `UseRouting` placement.

The issue: my `Program.cs` calls `app.MapHealthChecks("/ready")` then `app.MapGet("/")` then `app.MapControllers()`, then `UseHttpsRedirection`/`UseRouting`/`UseAuthorization`/`UseOcelot()`. With `UseOcelot()` *after* `UseRouting`, Ocelot intercepts every request. The correct order is to use **terminal middleware** to short-circuit the pipeline, or call `UseOcelot()` *before* `UseRouting`.

The right pattern in ASP.NET Core with Ocelot is:
1. `app.UseOcelot().Wait()` — this calls `UseRouting` internally and is the first middleware
2. OR map Ocelot routes using `MapWhen` etc.

But we still need `/ready` to bypass Ocelot. The cleanest fix: handle `/ready` with a **branching middleware** that runs *before* `UseOcelot()`:

The key insight: `app.MapWhen` with a predicate that matches `/ready` will create a branch where the inner middleware pipeline is isolated. Within that branch, we can map the health endpoints. The main pipeline (non-matched requests) goes to Ocelot.

But the issue was that `app.MapHealthChecks` inside `appBuilder` was failing because `appBuilder` is `ApplicationBuilder`, not `IEndpointRouteBuilder`. 

Actually, I need to reconsider this. `MapWhen` passes an `ApplicationBuilder` to its callback, and `MapHealthChecks` requires an `IEndpointRouteBuilder` which `ApplicationBuilder` does implement. The cleanest way to handle this is creating a separate `IApplicationBuilder` for the health endpoints, then using `MapWhen` to route requests based on the path—sending `/ready`, `/health`, and `/` to the health endpoints branch while everything else goes through Ocelot. I'm realizing the simplest approach might be to just handle the health check directly in middleware before Ocelot even processes the request, rather than trying to route it through the pipeline.

**Gateway ([Program.cs](backend/Services/APIGateway/Program.cs)):**
- Removed MMLib.SwaggerForOcelot — using pure Swashbuckle with `AddSwaggerGen()` defining all 11 service docs
- Added `app.UseSwagger()` and `app.UseSwaggerUI()` with manual `SwaggerEndpoint` mapping to all downstream `/swagger/{service}/swagger.json` URLs

**ocelot.json:** Added 11 upstream routes `/swagger/{service}/swagger.json` → downstream `service:8080/swagger/v1/swagger.json` (GET only)

- [Program.cs](backend/Services/UserService/Program.cs) + 9 others: Added `AddEndpointsApiExplorer()`, `AddSwaggerGen()`, `app.UseSwagger()`, `app.UseSwaggerUI()`

```bash
docker build --no-cache -t api-gateway:latest -f backend/Services/APIGateway/Dockerfile .
kubectl rollout restart deployment/cue-services-api-gateway -n cue
kubectl port-forward -n cue svc/api-gateway 8080:8080

```
